docs.title: Fannar
docs.text:
Representation spaces of trained models from Gram matrices of several sources: one positive-definite kernel per source of information, admissible transformations, Hadamard composition, and the geometry and spectral energy of the resulting matrix.

Fannar is the name of the method, and this library is its implementation. Both are described in the paper Building Spaces via Similarity Tensors in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces: A Mechanistic Interpretability Method.

pip install fannar            # core: numpy + matplotlib
pip install "fannar[all]"     # + PyTorch, scikit-learn and pandas

docs.title: The idea in one line
docs.text:
\[ G \;=\; T\big(\,T_1(K_1) \circ T_2(K_2) \circ \cdots \circ T_d(K_d)\,\big) \]

\(K_l\) is the raw Gram matrix of source \(l\) (from a kernel, or one you supply), \(T_l\) the component transform, \(\circ\) the Hadamard product and \(T\) the final transform. By the Schur product theorem, \(G\) is positive semidefinite for any such choice, so it defines a geometry (distances, neighbourhoods, level sets) and a spectral decomposition of energy. Everything Fannar reports is read from \(G\).

The library keeps apart, as the paper does:

  • the method: the construction above and the readings on \(G\) (KernelPipeline, GramSpace);
  • the instantiation: which objects, which sources, which kernels and transformations (TorchSources, TreeSources, or a function of yours).

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
A ResNet-18 trained with a small mark on 95% of the dog photos learns the shortcut and calls 40% of the marked cats dogs. In that model, half of Fannar's energy map falls on the mark, which covers 2% of the image; in the clean model, 91% falls on the animal. Confident errors. 113 of the 136 errors of a churn network come with more than 90% confidence; the geometric margin flags 55 of them. Pair explanations (XGBoost). What separates a rejected applicant from a similar approved one; where Fannar, SHAP and LIME agree, the conclusion is firmer.

Note

These examples come from models trained to illustrate the method, one run each; the systematic evaluation is in the paper. More case studies, and the interpretability service, at fannar.fernandocsdm.com.

docs.title: The method
docs.text: Fannar describes what a trained model does with a set of objects (test samples, positions of an image, tokens) through a single positive semidefinite matrix \(G \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), built from several sources of information about each object.

docs.title: The construction
docs.text:
\[ G \;=\; T\big(\,T_1(K_1) \circ T_2(K_2) \circ \cdots \circ T_d(K_d)\,\big) \]
  1. Sources. For every object \(i\) and source \(l\) there is an array \(x_i^{(l)}\): the activations of a layer, a gradient, the path through a tree, or anything else.
  2. Kernels. Each source gets a positive-definite kernel \(\kappa_l\), which gives the raw Gram matrix \(K_l[i, j] = \kappa_l(x_i^{(l)}, x_j^{(l)})\). You may also supply \(K_l\) directly.
  3. Component transforms. Each \(K_l\) goes through an admissible transformation \(T_l\).
  4. Hadamard composition. The components are multiplied entry by entry.
  5. Final transform. An admissible \(T\) normalises the product.

A transformation is admissible when it maps symmetric PSD matrices to symmetric PSD matrices and does not depend on the order of the objects, \(T(PGP^\top) = P\,T(G)\,P^\top\) for every permutation \(P\). Admissible transformations are closed under composition, and by the Schur product theorem the Hadamard product of PSD matrices is PSD. So \(G\) is PSD for any choice of kernels and admissible transforms: there are vectors \(\phi_i\) with \(G_{ij} = \langle \phi_i, \phi_j \rangle\), and everything below is computed from \(G\) alone, never from the \(\phi_i\).

docs.title: The instantiation of the paper
docs.text:
The default pipeline ("paper", or fa.paper_pipeline()) uses, for each source:

  • the linear kernel \(\kappa(x, y) = \langle x, y \rangle\);
  • the angular transform \(T_a(K) = D^{-1/2} K D^{-1/2}\) (cosine similarity, unit diagonal), followed by a shift \(\tfrac12 (T_a(K) + J)\), which moves the cosine into \([0, 1]\) and keeps the product of several components from collapsing to the identity;

and, after the Hadamard product, centring followed by trace normalisation, \(T = T_{tr} \circ T_c\).

Why linear kernels

With linear-type kernels, the Hadamard product realises the tensor product of the feature spaces, so the joint similarity keeps the multiplicative interaction between sources. Gaussian kernels lose it: the product of Gaussians is the Gaussian of the summed exponents, and the composition becomes an additive combination of the source metrics. RBF is available, but Linear and Cosine are the defaults for this reason.

docs.title: Sources of a neural network
docs.text:
For a PyTorch classifier, TorchSources extracts three sources at every probed layer, with one forward and one backward pass per batch:

source what it is activations the layer output \(A\), pooled to a common grid of positions gradients the derivative of the contrastive margin \(m = f_c - \frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{c' \neq c} f_{c'}\) with respect to that output parameters the filters the object activated, \(p[:, s] = \sum_c A[c, s]\, W[c, :]\), with \(W\) the weight that produces the output

Outputs of shape (N, C) give one position; (N, C, H, W) is pooled to grid × grid positions; (N, L, C) (tokens, with layout="tokens") is pooled over L. The default is grid=4.

Activations say what the layer represents, gradients how the decision depends on it, and parameters which part of the learned weights the object uses. Each source alone gives a different space; the product keeps only the similarity the three agree on.

docs.title: Two cautions the library enforces
docs.text:
The target of the gradient

With target="predicted", the gradient of each object is taken towards its own prediction, so the space already carries the decision and any reading about the decision becomes circular. The default is target="fixed": the margin of the same class (fixed_class, 0 by default) for every object.

The floor

Every reading needs a reference. Pass reference_model, the same architecture with its initial weights: the report then measures the geometry of that untrained network against the behaviour of the trained one. The only difference between a reading and its floor is training, so a reading below or at its floor says nothing about what was learned.

Untrained networks already have structure, so geometric readings on them can be far from chance. Without a floor it is impossible to tell structure that training created from structure the architecture and the data already had.

docs.title: What is read from G
docs.text:
Geometry. \(G\) defines a pseudometric

\[ d(i, j)^2 = G_{ii} + G_{jj} - 2\,G_{ij}, \]

and with it neighbourhoods, level sets \(\Gamma_r(i) = \{ j : d(i, j) = r \}\) and classes of objects the space cannot tell apart (\(d = 0\)).

Spectrum. With \(G = V \Lambda V^\top\), the energy of object \(i\) in mode \(k\) is \(E_{ik} = \lambda_k V_{ik}^2\), and each row sums to \(G_{ii}\). The first \(r\) modes form the retained subspace \(V_r\); by default \(r\) is the participation rank

\[ r = \operatorname{round}\!\left( \frac{(\operatorname{tr} G)^2}{\lVert G \rVert_F^2} \right), \]

which needs no eigendecomposition. Each object then splits into retained energy \(E_\parallel\) and orthogonal energy \(E_\perp\), and

\[ E_{\text{ratio}}(i) = \frac{E_\perp(i)}{G_{ii}} \]

measures how much of the object lies outside the dominant structure of the space. The reading e_ratio_error_auc tests whether a high \(E_{\text{ratio}}\) signals where the model errs.

Readings. The readings relate this geometry to what the model does (its predictions, errors and confusions), never only to the dataset's labels. See Readings and reports.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Every script below runs offline in a few seconds on a CPU. They use datasets that ship with scikit-learn, or synthetic data, so nothing is downloaded. The outputs shown are what each script prints with the seeds it sets. Your numbers may differ slightly across PyTorch versions.

pip install "fannar[all]"
git clone https://github.com/FernandoCsm-Knight/Fannar.git && cd Fannar/examples
python tabular_wine.py
script module model and data what it shows quickstart_digits.py fannar.tabular MLP, digits as 64 features the full tour: report, plots, pairs, swap test tabular_wine.py fannar.tabular MLP, wine as a DataFrame pandas input, named classes, pairs, errors tree_wine.py fannar.tree decision tree, wine, text labels depths as layers, slack scale, a tree as the floor image_digits_cnn.py fannar.image CNN, digits as 8×8 images DataLoader input, energy map of one image text_keywords.py fannar.text small transformer, synthetic sentences wrap_hf, automatic layers, energy per token custom_gram.py fannar no model your own sources, kernels and Gram matrices

docs.title: A table, with pandas
docs.text:
tabular_wine.py trains a small MLP on the 13 chemical measurements of the wine dataset. It passes the test DataFrame and a categorical Series straight to TabularInterpreter:

y = pd.Series(pd.Categorical.from_codes(data.target, ["barolo", "grignolino", "barbera"]))
...
interp = TabularInterpreter(model, X_te, y_te, layers=["block1", "block2"], reference_model=initial)
interp.feature_names[:4]   # ['alcohol', 'malic_acid', 'ash', 'alcalinity_of_ash']
interp.class_names         # ['barolo', 'grignolino', 'barbera']

The pair explanation says what separates a wine from the nearest one that the model puts in another class. The values are in the standardised scale the model was trained on:

par (0, 69): grignolino x barbera
  alcohol                        i = -1.08  j = +0.72  parcela 54%
  color_intensity                i = -1.05  j = -0.26  parcela 14%
  flavanoids                     i = -0.28  j = -1.22  parcela 11%

explain_errors aggregates the same reading over the three test errors. Compare each feature's share among the errors with its share in general. ash and magnesium weigh much more in the mistakes (18% and 15%) than in the model's decisions overall (11% and 5%):

  proline                        parcela nos erros 26% (em geral 25%), primeiro em 33%
  ash                            parcela nos erros 18% (em geral 11%), primeiro em 33%
  alcohol                        parcela nos erros 17% (em geral 16%), primeiro em 33%
  magnesium                      parcela nos erros 15% (em geral 5%), primeiro em 0%

The swap test checks the ranking. Each method orders the features, the features are swapped one by one from \(x_i\) to \(x_j\), and a larger area means the prediction flips sooner. Here the method's order beats both the size of the difference and a random order:

{'method': 0.765, 'absdiff': 0.669, 'random': 0.296, 'pairs': 20, 'layer': 'block2'}

docs.title: The same table, with a tree
docs.text:
tree_wine.py fits a depth-4 DecisionTreeClassifier on the same data, with the labels as text. TreeInterpreter maps them to tree.classes_ (sorted: ['barbera', 'barolo', 'grignolino']). It uses the training standard deviation as the slack scale, and a tree fitted on shuffled labels as the floor:

shuffled = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, rng.permutation(y_tr))
interp = TreeInterpreter(tree, X_te, y_te, X_train=X_tr, reference_model=shuffled)
The space of each depth (columns) for the joint pipeline, the path alone and the floor. The classes come apart as the tree goes deeper. The path alone collapses every leaf to a point, so the slack is what spreads the objects inside a leaf. In the floor the classes stay mixed.

The pair explanation can be read per depth. The root splits on alcohol, and from depth 2 on the decision moves to od280/od315_of_diluted_wines:

par (0, 83): grignolino x barbera
  od280/od315_of_diluted_wines   i =    2.57  j =    1.82  parcela 83%
  flavanoids                     i =    1.75  j =    0.48  parcela 17%
parcelas por profundidade (atributo principal): {'depth1': 'alcohol', 'depth2': 'od280/...', ...}

docs.title: Images, and where the energy sits
docs.text:
image_digits_cnn.py reads the 8×8 digits as images (N, 1, 8, 8) and trains a three-block CNN (97% test accuracy). ImageInterpreter receives the test DataLoader as it is. Each block's output is pooled to a 4×4 grid, so conv3 has 32 channels × 16 positions per object.

For one image, energy_map uses the positions as the objects:

emap = interp.energy_map(image, "conv2")                 # (8, 8)
interp.plot_energy_map(image, "conv2", image=image[0])
Retained energy per position of conv2 over a "1". The stroke covers 36% of the image and holds 72% of the energy.

docs.title: Text, layer by layer
docs.text:
text_keywords.py builds sentences of 8 to 16 tokens with padding. The class is a keyword placed at a random position. The model mimics the Hugging Face interface (model(input_ids=..., attention_mask=...) returns an object with .logits), so the script uses wrap_hf as it would with a real model. It does not pass layers=, so the three encoder blocks are found automatically.

The per-token energy shows how the information moves through the network. In the first two blocks the keyword is the token with the most energy. In the last block, attention has already spread it over every token:

frase 0: palavra-chave na posição 6 de 12; energia por token (normalizada):
  model.encoder.layer.0  [0.27 0.75 0.05 0.05 0.03 0.17 1.   0.32 0.31 0.07 0.05 0.55]
  model.encoder.layer.1  [0.22 0.55 0.16 0.06 0.03 0.21 1.   0.3  0.22 0.17 0.23 0.09]
  model.encoder.layer.2  [0.97 0.66 0.99 0.83 0.81 1.   0.99 0.97 0.92 0.95 0.94 0.91]

token de maior energia = palavra-chave (100 frases; ao acaso ~9%):
  model.encoder.layer.0  54%
  model.encoder.layer.1  66%
  model.encoder.layer.2  12%

Pick the layer for the question

Energy maps read the positions inside one layer. To see which tokens (or image regions) carry the information, look at the early and middle blocks. Near the output, attention and pooling have mixed the positions, and the map becomes uniform even when the model is right.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Fannar needs Python 3.10 or later. The core depends only on NumPy and Matplotlib; the model integrations are optional extras.

pip install fannar

import numpy as np

X = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((50, 8))

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page interprets a small PyTorch network trained on scikit-learn's digits dataset, layer by layer. The full script is examples/quickstart_digits.py.

pip install "fannar[all]"

docs.title: 1. Keep a copy of the untrained model
docs.text:
Every reading needs a reference to be meaningful. The natural one is the same network before training, so copy it before the first optimisation step:

import copy
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X = (X / 16.0).astype(np.float32)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=0)

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential()
model.add_module("block1", nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU()))
model.add_module("block2", nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU()))
model.add_module("block3", nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU()))
model.add_module("head", nn.Linear(64, 10))
initial = copy.deepcopy(model)            # the floor: the same network before training

docs.title: 2. Train as usual
docs.text:
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 1e-3)
xt, yt = torch.from_numpy(X_tr), torch.from_numpy(y_tr)
for epoch in range(60):
    for idx in torch.randperm(len(xt)).split(64):
        opt.zero_grad()
        nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(xt[idx]), yt[idx]).backward()
        opt.step()
model.eval()

docs.title: 3. Build the interpreter
docs.text:
Each 64-pixel image is a row of 64 features here, so the entry point is fannar.tabular:

import fannar as fa
from fannar.tabular import TabularInterpreter

interp = TabularInterpreter(
    model, X_te, y_te,                        # the trained model and the objects to interpret
    layers=["block1", "block2", "block3"],    # names from model.named_modules()
    reference_model=initial,                  # optional, but recommended: the floor
    feature_names=[f"pixel{t}" for t in range(64)],
)

TabularInterpreter is an fa.Interpreter with defaults for tables. fa.Interpreter takes the same arguments and gives the same numbers. For images, token sequences and trees, see Choosing a module.

Nothing is computed yet. The first call that needs the spaces runs interp.fit(), which extracts the sources of every layer in one pass over X_te and builds one GramSpace per layer.

docs.title: 4. Read the report
docs.text:
report = interp.evaluate()
print(f"test accuracy: {report.meta['accuracy']:.3f}")
print(report.to_markdown())               # also report.to_frame() and report.to_json("r.json")
interp.plot_report(report)                # readings × layers

For each layer the report holds the readings of three representations:

  • joint: the method, with the three sources combined;
  • activations: a baseline with the activations alone;
  • floor: the same pipeline on the untrained network, measured against the trained network's behaviour.

A reading only says something about training when joint is above floor. What each reading asks is described in Readings and reports.

docs.title: 5. Look at the spaces
docs.text:
interp.plot_embedding()                   # each layer on its two dominant modes
interp.plot_gram("block2")                # component Grams, Hadamard product, final Gram
interp.plot_spectrum("block2")            # eigenvalues and participation rank

space = interp.space("block2")            # the GramSpace itself
space.neighbors(0, 5)
space.energies()["E_ratio"]

docs.title: 6. Explain decisions
docs.text:
expl = interp.explain_pair(0)             # object 0 vs. its nearest object with another prediction
for name, vi, vj, share in expl.top(5):
    print(f"{name:8s} i = {vi:.2f}  j = {vj:.2f}  share {share:.0%}")
expl.plot()

errs = interp.explain_errors()            # which features keep the errors away from their class
errs.top(5)
errs.plot()

interp.swap_test(30, layer="block3")      # validation outside the geometry

See Explanations for what these numbers mean and how they are validated.

docs.title: Saving figures
docs.text:
Every plot_* method returns a Matplotlib figure:

interp.plot_report(report).savefig("report.png", dpi=150)

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
With \(n\) objects, \(D\) the total dimension of the sources and \(F\) the number of input features:

step cost one Gram matrix (kernels, transforms, Hadamard product) \(\Theta(n^2 D)\) distances, neighbours, centring, participation rank \(\Theta(n^2)\) full spectral decomposition (energies, embedding, containment) \(\Theta(n^3)\), computed once per space a pair explanation one forward and one backward pass over \(F + 2\) rows a swap-test curve one forward pass over \(F + 1\) rows

The spectral transforms (whiten, spectral, psd_project, max_eig_normalize) also cost \(\Theta(n^3)\); the others are \(O(n^2)\).

docs.title: Keeping it fast
docs.text:
• Number of objects. Memory and time grow with \(n^2\) and \(n^3\). A few thousand objects per space is comfortable on a laptop; subsample X beyond that.
  • Grid. For convolutional and token layers, grid (default 4) sets how many positions are kept per axis, so \(D\) grows with C × grid². Lower it for wide layers.
  • Sources. sources=("activations", "gradients") skips the parameter source, the largest for layers with many inputs per channel.
  • Device and batch size. Extraction runs on the model's device in batches of batch_size=256; the Gram algebra runs on the CPU in float64.
  • Errors. explain_errors(max_errors=..., reference=...) caps how many pairs are explained.

docs.title: Your own Gram matrices
docs.text: The construction does not depend on neural networks. Any set of objects with one or more sources of information can go through a KernelPipeline, and any component can be your kernel, your transform, or a matrix you already computed. The full script is examples/custom_gram.py.

docs.title: A pipeline
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import fannar as fa

pipe = fa.KernelPipeline(
    {
        "state":  fa.Component(fa.Linear(), fa.angular() >> fa.shift(1.0)),
        "text":   fa.Component(fa.RBF(gamma=0.1), fa.identity),
        "mine":   fa.Component(lambda A, B: (A @ B.T + 1) ** 2),   # any function k(X, Y)
    },
    final=fa.center >> fa.trace_normalize,
)

space = pipe(sources={"state": S, "text": T, "mine": M}, labels=y)

Each source is an array whose first axis indexes the objects; the other axes are flattened. NumPy arrays, PyTorch tensors and lists are accepted.

There are three shorter ways to declare the components:

fa.KernelPipeline(["a", "b"])                     # default component for each name
fa.KernelPipeline({"a": "linear", "b": "cosine"}) # a kernel name per source
fa.KernelPipeline({"a": fa.Polynomial(degree=3)}) # a kernel object per source

The default component is the one of the paper: linear kernel, then angular() >> shift(1.0). The default final transform is center >> trace_normalize.

docs.title: Matrices you already have
docs.text:
A raw Gram passed in grams takes precedence over the kernel applied to sources, so you can replace any component, or all of them:

space = pipe(sources={"state": S, "text": T}, grams={"mine": K_mine})   # mix
space = pipe(grams={"state": K1, "text": K2, "mine": K3})               # matrices only

The component transform is still applied to a matrix given in grams. To skip the construction altogether, build the space directly from any PSD matrix:

space = fa.GramSpace(my_psd_matrix, labels=y)

With an Interpreter, interp.space_from_grams({...}) does the same with the model's labels and predictions attached.

docs.title: Kernels
Transforms
docs.text:
Transforms compose with >>, from left to right: fa.center >> fa.trace_normalize centres and then normalises.

transform effect cost identity \(G\) center \(HGH\), with \(H = I - \frac1n J\) \(O(n^2)\) trace_normalize \(G / \operatorname{tr} G\) \(O(n)\) frobenius_normalize \(G / \lVert G \rVert_F\) \(O(n^2)\) max_eig_normalize \(G / \lambda_{\max}\) \(O(n^3)\) angular(eps=1e-12) \(D^{-1/2} G D^{-1/2}\) (unit diagonal; 0 for null objects) \(O(n^2)\) shift(c=1.0) \((G + cJ)/(1 + c)\), c >= 0 \(O(n^2)\) whiten(tol=1e-10) projector onto the range of \(G\) \(O(n^3)\) spectral(f) \(V f(\Lambda) V^\top\), with \(f \ge 0\) on \(\lambda \ge 0\) \(O(n^3)\) psd_project() nearest PSD matrix (negative eigenvalues set to 0) \(O(n^3)\)

identity, center, trace_normalize, frobenius_normalize and max_eig_normalize are transform objects; the others are functions that return one, so they take parentheses.

A transform of your own is any function of a symmetric matrix wrapped in Transform. It is your responsibility that it is admissible (PSD in, PSD out, independent of the order of the objects):

sqrt_spectrum = fa.spectral(np.sqrt, name="sqrt")         # V Λ^{1/2} Vᵀ
square = fa.Transform(lambda G: G * G, "hadamard_square")  # PSD by the Schur product theorem

component = fa.Component(fa.Linear(), fa.angular() >> square)

Entry-wise functions are the usual trap: most of them (np.log1p, np.sqrt entry by entry) do not keep a matrix PSD.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
preset what it is fa.paper_pipeline(sources=("parameters", "activations", "gradients"), shift_by=1.0) the instantiation of the paper fa.single_source("activations", angular_shift=True) one source with the paper's component transform, for ablations fa.single_source(..., angular_shift=False) the plain linear centred Gram: Euclidean distances, the geometry of linear CKA and RSA fa.positions_pipeline(sources) positions of one input as objects (used by the energy maps)

Wherever a pipeline is expected, the names in fa.PRESETS also work: "paper", "activations", "gradients", "parameters", "euclidean".

docs.title: The Hadamard root
docs.text: KernelPipeline(..., root=True) takes the \(d\)-th Hadamard root of the product of \(d\) components before the final transform: the entry-wise geometric mean of the components. Fractional Hadamard powers do not preserve positive semidefiniteness, so the result is projected back on the PSD cone, and the fraction of spectral mass that projection discarded is stored in space.info["root_discarded"].

docs.title: Inspecting a pipeline
docs.text:
print(pipe)                       # kernels and transforms of every component
grams = pipe.component_grams(sources={...})   # T_l(K_l) for each component
space.components                  # the same, kept on the space (unless keep_components=False)
space.info["pipeline"]

docs.title: Explanations
docs.text: Beyond the readings on whole spaces, Fannar explains individual decisions by contrast: why does the model place object \(i\) apart from object \(j\)? Pair explanations need vector inputs, X of shape (n, F).

docs.title: Pairs
docs.text:
For a pair \((i, j)\) and each feature \(f\), let \(x_i^{(f)}\) be \(x_i\) with feature \(f\) replaced by its value in \(x_j\). The score of \(f\) in a layer is

\[ \Delta d_f = d(i, j) - d\big(i^{(f)}, j\big), \]

measured in that layer's representation space. A positive \(\Delta d_f\) means the swap brings \(i\) closer to \(j\): the feature is part of what separates them for the model. Only the \(F + 2\) rows \(x_j, x_i, x_i^{(1)}, \dots, x_i^{(F)}\) go through the model, so the cost is linear in the number of features.

expl = interp.explain_pair(i)          # j = nearest object (in input space) with another prediction
expl = interp.explain_pair(i, j)       # or an explicit partner
expl.j, expl.pred_i, expl.pred_j

expl.top(5)                            # [(feature, x_i, x_j, share), ...], last layer
expl.top(5, layer="layer2")
expl.ranking(), expl.shares()          # indices, and positive scores normalised to sum 1
expl.scores["layer2"]                  # raw Δd per feature
expl.to_frame()                        # pandas
expl.plot(k=8)                         # share per layer (heatmap) and the values of i and j

First order

\(\Delta d_f\) swaps one feature at a time. Features that only matter together with others get no credit.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
explain_errors aggregates pair explanations over the model's mistakes. Each misclassified object \(i\) is paired with the nearest object the model gets right in the true class of \(i\), so the shares say which features keep the error away from where it belongs.

errs = interp.explain_errors()                 # against="correct" (default) or "unlike"
errs = interp.explain_errors(max_errors=200, reference=100, seed=0)

errs.top(5)                    # [(feature, mean share, fraction of errors where it is first)]
errs.mean_shares()             # per feature, over the errors
errs.reference_shares()        # the same over correctly predicted objects: the general importance
errs.direction()               # +1: errors have lower values than their partners; −1: higher
errs.confusions()              # [(true, predicted, count)], most frequent first
errs.by_class(), errs.by_confusion()
errs.pairs                     # [(error, partner)], e.g. for swap_test
errs.to_frame()
errs.plot(rows="class")        # or rows="confusion"

Compare mean_shares() with reference_shares(): a feature with a high share among the errors but a low one in general is specific to the mistakes.

docs.title: Validating with the swap test
docs.text:
The pair ranking is validated outside the geometry. Copy the top-\(k\) features of \(j\) into \(i\), for \(k = 0, \dots, F\), and check whether the model's prediction becomes the prediction of \(j\); the area under that curve is higher when the ranking finds the decisive features sooner. This is the procedure of nearest-instance counterfactuals such as NICE.

interp.swap_test(50, layer="layer3")
# {"method": <area>, "absdiff": <area>, "random": <area>, "pairs": 50, "layer": "layer3"}

interp.swap_test(errs.pairs[:30])     # explicit pairs

method ranks by \(\Delta d\), absdiff by \(|x_j - x_i|\), and random shuffles the features that differ. The method's ranking is useful where it beats both. With an integer, the pairs are random correctly predicted objects, each with its nearest object of another prediction.

docs.title: Energy maps
docs.text:
For a single input with spatial structure (an image, a series, a sequence of tokens), the positions of that input can be the objects. energy_map builds the space of the positions of one layer and returns the retained energy \(E_\parallel\) of each one:

emap = interp.energy_map(x, "layer2", max_side=32)   # (h, w) for images, (L,) for sequences
interp.plot_energy_map(x, "layer2", image=rgb)       # rgb: (H, W[, 3]) in [0, 1]

The components use linear kernels without the angular transform, which would give every position the same energy (fa.positions_pipeline()). max_side caps the grid, since the Gram is \(P \times P\) for \(P\) positions. Energy maps need a PyTorch model.

docs.title: The representation space
docs.text:
A GramSpace holds the final matrix \(G\) of \(n\) objects and everything read from it. You get one from a pipeline, from interp.space(layer), or directly from any symmetric PSD matrix:

space = fa.GramSpace(G, labels=y, predictions=pred)
space.n, space.is_psd(), space.G

The input is symmetrised. Labels and predictions are optional and only stored for the readings and the plots.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
\(G\) defines the pseudometric \(d(i, j)^2 = G_{ii} + G_{jj} - 2G_{ij}\): the distance between the implicit feature vectors \(\phi_i\) and \(\phi_j\).

space.distances               # (n, n) matrix, computed once
space.distance(i, j)
space.neighbors(i, k)         # the k nearest objects to i, nearest first
space.level_band(i, r, delta) # Γ_{r,δ}(i) = { j : |d(i, j) − r| ≤ δ }
space.level_set(i, r)         # Γ_r(i), up to a tolerance
space.equivalence_classes()   # groups of objects the space cannot tell apart (d = 0)
space.subset(idx)             # the sub-space of some objects (not re-transformed)

It is a pseudometric: two different objects can be at distance zero. That happens, for instance, in a tree layer where two objects took the same path with the same slack. equivalence_classes() lists those groups.

docs.title: Spectrum and energy
docs.text:
space.eigenvalues             # descending, clipped at zero
space.eigenvectors            # columns in the same order
space.eigenvalues_raw         # ascending, unclipped: negative values reveal a non-PSD input
space.participation_rank()    # round((tr G)² / ‖G‖²_F), O(n²)
space.rank("tau", tau=0.95)   # modes holding 95% of the energy
space.mode_energy()           # (n, n): E_ik = λ_k V_ik², rows sum to G_ii

energies() splits each object's energy between the retained subspace \(V_r\) and its orthogonal complement:

e = space.energies()          # r = participation rank; or energies(5), energies("tau", 0.9)
e["rank"]                     # r
e["E_par"], e["E_perp"]       # retained and orthogonal energy per object
e["E_total"]                  # = diag(G)
e["E_ratio"]                  # E_perp / E_total
e["retained_fraction"]        # share of the trace in the first r modes

The rank argument accepts "participation" (default), "tau" or an explicit integer.

docs.title: Embedding
docs.text:
coords, retained = space.embedding(2)   # sqrt(λ_k) V_ik on the two dominant modes

This is kernel PCA of \(G\): with all modes, coords @ coords.T reproduces \(G\). retained is the fraction of the trace the shown modes carry; read a 2-D picture with that number in mind.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
space.containment(labels)     # in [0, 1]

The fraction of the centred class-indicator directions that lies inside \(V_r\). By default \(r = K - 1\) (number of classes minus one), which makes the value comparable across spaces; the participation rank of each space is not.

docs.title: Comparing spaces
docs.text:
space.cka(other)              # centred kernel alignment, other: GramSpace or array
parts = space.decompose(K)    # Ĝ = a·K̂ + R
parts["alignment"]            # a = CKA(G, K)
parts["seen"]                 # GramSpace of the part K explains
parts["residual"]             # GramSpace of what K does not explain (projected on the PSD cone)
parts["discarded"]            # spectral mass lost in that projection

decompose answers "what does this space contain beyond the reference?". With K the activations-only Gram, for example, the residual is the part of the joint space that the activations alone do not explain.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
from fannar import plots

plots.plot_gram(space, order_by=y)   # components, their product, and G
plots.plot_spectrum(space)           # eigenvalues, cumulative energy, participation rank

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
fannar.image interprets PyTorch image classifiers (CNNs, residual networks, vision transformers whose blocks return (N, C, H, W)). ImageInterpreter is an Interpreter with defaults for images.

from fannar.image import ImageInterpreter

interp = ImageInterpreter(
    model, test_loader, y_test,               # array, tensor or DataLoader
    layers=["layer1", "layer2", "layer3"],
    reference_model=initial,
    class_names=classes,
)
report = interp.evaluate()
interp.plot_embedding()

X can be an array, a tensor or a DataLoader (the first element of each batch is used, so (image, label) batches work as they are).

docs.title: Pooling
docs.text: A convolutional output (N, C, H, W) is average-pooled to grid × grid positions, so each object has C × grid² values per source. ImageInterpreter uses grid=4. A larger grid keeps more spatial detail, but the size of the sources (and the cost) grows with grid². grid=None keeps every position.

docs.title: Where the energy sits inside one image
docs.text:
With images as objects there are no per-feature explanations (explain_pair needs vector inputs). To see which parts of one image carry the model's energy, use the positions of that image as the objects:

emap = interp.energy_map(image, "layer2")           # (h, w) retained energy per position
interp.plot_energy_map(image, "layer2", image=rgb)  # over the picture, values in [0, 1]

max_side (default 32) caps the grid of positions, since the Gram matrix is P × P. The map has the resolution of the probed layer: after two stride-2 stages a block's map is 4 times smaller per side than the input, and plot_energy_map stretches it over the picture.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: examples/image_digits_cnn.py trains a three-block CNN on the 8×8 digits and draws the energy map of one image. See Examples.

docs.title: Things to watch
docs.text:
• Name the blocks. The layers are module names. With nn.Sequential and anonymous children they are "0", "1"… Name the blocks (add_module("conv1", ...)) or look them up in dict(model.named_modules()).
  • Probe the block, not a lone ReLU. Probing a block's output gives the state the next block reads. The parameter source is found inside the block (the last convolution with as many output channels). If it is not, pass weight_modules={"layer": "path.to.conv"}.
  • Batch norm and dropout. The extraction puts the model in eval() mode and restores it afterwards, so batch statistics are not updated.
  • Memory. The sources hold n × C × grid² values per layer and source. For wide layers, lower grid or the number of objects before raising anything else.

docs.title: Choosing a module
docs.text:
Since 0.4.0 there is one entry point per kind of data. Each is a thin Interpreter with sensible defaults and the same methods, and it gives the same numbers as fa.Interpreter with the same options:

data / model module class guide PyTorch model on tabular rows fannar.tabular TabularInterpreter Tabular data PyTorch CNN or ViT on images fannar.image ImageInterpreter Images PyTorch transformer on tokens (Hugging Face included) fannar.text TextInterpreter Text scikit-learn decision tree fannar.tree TreeInterpreter Decision trees anything else fannar Interpreter(extractor=...) below 
import fannar as fa
fa.tabular.TabularInterpreter    # the modules load on first access; no extra import needed

fa.Interpreter still picks the sources from the type of the model, as in earlier versions:

model sources "layers" torch.nn.Module TorchSources: activations, gradients, parameters the modules in layers scikit-learn tree (has tree_ and decision_path) TreeSources: path, slack, classes each depth, depth1 … depthD anything else your extractor function whatever your function returns

docs.title: PyTorch options
docs.text:
These options apply to TabularInterpreter, ImageInterpreter, TextInterpreter and to fa.Interpreter with a PyTorch model. Any classifier that returns logits (N, K) works. Name the modules to probe as they appear in model.named_modules(); with layers=None, every direct child that has parameters is probed.

interp = fa.Interpreter(model, X_test, y_test, layers=["layer1", "layer2", "layer3"],
                        reference_model=initial)

X can be an array, a tensor or a DataLoader (the first element of each batch is used). The keyword arguments that Interpreter does not know are passed to TorchSources:

option default meaning target "fixed" class of the contrastive margin: "fixed", "predicted" or an int fixed_class 0 the class used by target="fixed" grid 4 (8 in TextInterpreter) positions kept per spatial or token axis (None keeps all) layout "channels" ("tokens" in TextInterpreter) "tokens" for outputs shaped (N, L, C) sources all three a subset of ("parameters", "activations", "gradients") weight_modules automatic {layer: module or name} whose weight defines the parameter source margin "contrastive" or a callable fn(logits, target) -> (N,) device, batch_size model's device, 256

docs.title: The parameter source
docs.text: The parameter source needs the weight W that produces the probed output. By default it is the probed module's own weight or, inside a block, the last module up to it whose weight has as many rows as the output has channels (conv2 in a residual block, the Linear before a probed activation). When none fits, the parameter source is skipped with a warning; point to the right module with weight_modules={"layer": "path.to.module"}.

docs.title: Any other model
docs.text:
Give extractor, a function that returns the sources of a batch of objects and the model's predictions:

def sources(X):
    layers = {"output": {"proba": model.predict_proba(X), "leaves": model.apply(X)}}
    return layers, model.predict(X)                 # optionally a third item: probabilities

interp = fa.Interpreter(model, X_test, y_test, extractor=sources,
                        pipeline=fa.KernelPipeline(["proba", "leaves"]),
                        baselines={})

The function can return (layers, predictions), (layers, predictions, probabilities) or a Sources object. layers maps each layer name to {source name: array}, with the objects on the first axis. The probabilities feed the soft confusion of the confusion_agreement reading; without them the confusion is counted.

The default baseline is the activations source alone. It is skipped in the layers where your function provides no activations, so pass baselines={} to say so explicitly, or baselines built from the sources you do provide.

Pair explanations with your own extractor

explain_pair, explain_errors and swap_test call your function on new rows (the object with one feature swapped), so it must work on any (m, F) float32 array, not only on X_test. swap_test also needs predict=, a function returning labels, for models that are neither PyTorch nor scikit-learn trees.

docs.title: Readings and reports
docs.text: A reading relates a representation space to the behaviour of the model: its predictions, its errors, its confusions. The claim under test is that the geometry reflects what this model does, not that it separates the dataset's classes, so the reference is always something the model produced.

docs.title: The readings
docs.text:
reading question range knn_prediction Do an object's \(k\) nearest neighbours share its prediction? (leave-one-out, against the model's predictions) \([0, 1]\) correctness_auc Does the geometric margin anticipate where the model is wrong? AUC, 0.5 = chance confusion_agreement Are the classes the model confuses close to each other? (Spearman, \(\ge 5\) classes) \([-1, 1]\) containment Are the class directions inside the retained subspace \(V_r\), \(r = K - 1\)? \([0, 1]\) e_ratio_error_auc Does the energy outside \(V_r\) signal the errors? AUC, 0.5 = chance rank participation rank of the space (context, not a reading)

Geometric margin. For object \(i\), with \(\bar d_{\text{own}}\) the mean distance to the objects of its predicted class and \(\bar d_{\text{near}}\) the mean distance to the closest other class,

\[ \text{margin}(i) = \frac{\bar d_{\text{near}} - \bar d_{\text{own}}}{\bar d_{\text{near}} + \bar d_{\text{own}}} \in [-1, 1]. \]

The margin groups objects by the model's predictions; the true labels only define the target (right or wrong). Using the labels in the margin too would make the reading circular, and would rely on a signal that does not exist when the model is deployed.

Confusion. With probabilities, the confusion between classes \(a\) and \(b\) is the mean probability the model gives to \(b\) on objects of \(a\), symmetrised. It is informative even when the model rarely errs. Without probabilities, the errors are counted.

Readings that need errors (correctness_auc, e_ratio_error_auc) are NaN when the model makes fewer than 5 errors, or fewer than 5 correct predictions, on the sample.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
interp.evaluate() computes every reading for every layer and representation and returns a Report:

report = interp.evaluate(layers=None, include_baselines=True, include_floor=True)

report.layers                 # ["layer1", "layer2", ...]
report.representations        # ["joint", "activations", "floor"]
report.values["joint"]["layer2"]["correctness_auc"]
report.series("correctness_auc", "joint")         # one value per layer
report.above_floor("correctness_auc")             # bool per layer (None without a floor)
report.meta                   # accuracy, n, pipeline
representation what it is joint the interpreter's pipeline (by default, the paper's three sources) one per baseline each pipeline in baselines (by default, activations alone) floor the joint pipeline on reference_model, against the trained model's behaviour

Read against the floor

A reading is evidence about training only where it is above its floor. Untrained networks already produce structured spaces, and some readings are far from chance on them.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
print(report.to_markdown(digits=3))   # one table per reading, layers as columns
report.to_json("report.json")         # also returns the text
df = report.to_frame()                # long format: representation, layer, reading, value
report.plot()                         # same as interp.plot_report(report)

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
Any pipeline or preset name can be a baseline. Use a dictionary to name them:

interp = fa.Interpreter(model, X, y, layers=layers,
                        baselines={"acts": "activations", "grads": "gradients",
                                   "euclid": "euclidean"})

docs.title: Readings on any space
docs.text:
The readings also work on a space you built yourself:

from fannar import readings

values = fa.evaluate(space, labels, predictions, probabilities=None, k=5)
readings.correctness_auc(space, labels, predictions)
readings.geometric_margin(space, predictions)        # per object
readings.class_distance_matrix(space, labels)        # (K, K) mean distances, classes

docs.title: Tabular data
docs.text:
fannar.tabular interprets a PyTorch model that reads rows of features (an MLP, a residual MLP, a model for tabular data). TabularInterpreter is an Interpreter that accepts pandas objects directly. The construction of the space is the same.

from fannar.tabular import TabularInterpreter

interp = TabularInterpreter(
    model, df_test, y_test,                   # DataFrame and labels
    layers=["block1", "block2", "block3"],    # names from model.named_modules()
    reference_model=initial,                  # the same network before training (the floor)
)
report = interp.evaluate()
interp.explain_errors().top(5)                # features named after df_test.columns
interp.explain_pair(0).top(5)
interp.swap_test(30)

What changes compared with fa.Interpreter:

input what TabularInterpreter does X is a DataFrame its columns become feature_names; the values are converted to float32 y is a categorical Series the category codes are the labels and the categories are class_names y holds strings encoded by sorted unique value (the order of scikit-learn's LabelEncoder) y is numeric used as is: the model's output indices 0 … K-1

Explicit feature_names= and class_names= take precedence. The label encoding must match the one used to train the model. Pass integer labels when in doubt.

Nothing is preprocessed. Pass the rows in the scale the model was trained on (for instance, already standardised). Every other keyword (target, fixed_class, device, batch_size, pipeline, baselines, k) works as in Interpreter and PyTorch options.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: examples/tabular_wine.py trains an MLP on scikit-learn's wine and walks through pandas input, pair and error explanations and the swap test. Its output is discussed in Examples.

docs.title: Things to watch
docs.text:
• Scale. The pair explanations swap raw values between rows. If the model was trained on standardised features, pass standardised rows, and the values in top() are standardised too.
  • Label order. With string labels, the sorted order must be the one used to train the model. When the model was trained with its own encoding, pass integer labels and class_names= explicitly.
  • Errors. explain_errors() raises ValueError when the model makes no errors on X. Use a held-out set; the training rows of a well-fitted model may have none.
  • Cost. Each pair runs \(F + 2\) rows through the model, so explaining every error of a large test set with many features takes a while. Cap it with max_errors= (see Cost).

For a scikit-learn decision tree on the same table, use fannar.tree.

docs.title: Text and token sequences
docs.text: fannar.text interprets PyTorch models whose hidden states are token sequences (N, L, C): transformer encoders, Hugging Face classifiers, or any model with a sequence axis. TextInterpreter is an Interpreter that reads the channels on the last axis (layout="tokens") and pools the sequence to grid=8 positions.

docs.title: Hugging Face models
docs.text:
Hugging Face models take several inputs and return an object rather than a logits tensor. wrap_hf turns one into a module whose forward(input_ids) returns the logits and builds the attention mask from the padding token:

from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer
from fannar.text import TextInterpreter, wrap_hf

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
hf_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name).eval()
ids = tokenizer(texts, padding="max_length", truncation=True, max_length=128,
                return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]

model = wrap_hf(hf_model, pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id)
interp = TextInterpreter(model, ids, labels)        # layers: every encoder block
report = interp.evaluate()

transformers is not a dependency of Fannar. wrap_hf only needs the call model(input_ids=..., attention_mask=...) to return an object with .logits, a tuple or a tensor. Extra keyword arguments of wrap_hf are passed to every call of the model.

docs.title: Which layers
docs.text:
With layers=None, the probed layers are the blocks of the model's longest nn.ModuleList (encoder.layer.*, transformer.h.*, layers.*…), as returned by fannar.text.block_names:

from fannar.text import block_names
block_names(model)    # ['model.bert.encoder.layer.0', ..., 'model.bert.encoder.layer.11']

The wrapper stores the original model as model, so the names gain the prefix model.. Pass layers= to probe a subset. Blocks that return a tuple are probed on their first tensor.

docs.title: Pooling and token energy
docs.text:
Each hidden state is average-pooled along the sequence to grid positions. grid=None keeps every token, which requires sequences of the same length. interp.energy_map(ids[0], layer) returns the retained energy of every token of one sequence (the tokens are the objects). Slice off the padding before reading it: energy[: (ids[0] != pad).sum()].

Early and middle blocks for token maps

In the text example, the keyword that decides the class is the most energetic token in 54% and 66% of the sentences in the first two blocks (chance is about 9%). In the last block it is 12%, because attention has already spread the information over every token. Token maps answer "which tokens carry the information" best before the last blocks.

Your own model only has to take one tensor and return logits (N, K). In that case TextInterpreter(model, X, y, layers=[...]) works without wrap_hf.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: examples/text_keywords.py trains a three-block transformer on synthetic sentences, with the Hugging Face interface, and compares the token energy across blocks. See Examples.

docs.title: Things to watch
docs.text:
• Padding. Without pad_token_id, wrap_hf attends to every token, padding included, which is not how the model was trained. Pass the tokenizer's pad_token_id.
  • Same length. The objects go through the model in batches, so the sequences must be padded to the same length (padding="max_length" in the tokenizer).
  • Large models. Each layer and source keeps n × C × grid values. A 12-block model with C = 768 and grid=8 stores about 6 000 numbers per object, layer and source. Probe a subset of layers= and a few hundred objects first.
  • Reference model. For the floor, wrap the untrained copy too: reference_model=wrap_hf(initial, pad_token_id=...), so its layer names match.

docs.title: Decision trees
docs.text:
fannar.tree interprets a fitted scikit-learn DecisionTreeClassifier. A tree has no activations and no gradient, so it gets its own instantiation of the sources, one "layer" per depth. At depth \(l\) each object has:

  • path: indicator of the nodes visited up to depth \(l\) (the state of the tree);
  • slack: \((x_f - t)/\sigma_f\) at every internal node already crossed, i.e. how far the object is from switching branch (the tree's sensitivity);
  • classes: the class distribution of the node the object reaches at depth \(l\).
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from fannar.tree import TreeInterpreter

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5).fit(X_train, y_train)
interp = TreeInterpreter(tree, df_test, y_test, X_train=df_train)   # slack in training std units
report = interp.evaluate()
interp.explain_pair(0).top(5)
interp.explain_errors().top(5)

The joint pipeline is KernelPipeline(["path", "slack", "classes"]) and the baseline is the path alone.

argument meaning X_train training rows. Their per-feature standard deviation is \(\sigma_f\) in the slack scale an explicit per-feature \(\sigma_f\) (overrides X_train). Without either, \(\sigma_f = 1\) depths the depths used as layers (default 1 … max_depth) reference_model another tree (e.g. shallower or randomised) used as the floor

X can be a DataFrame (its columns become feature_names). The labels can be any of the tree's classes, strings included. They are mapped to indices into tree.classes_, which also become class_names, so the readings and explanations work for any label type.

fa.Interpreter(tree, X, y, scale=...) still works as in earlier versions.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: examples/tree_wine.py fits a depth-4 tree on wine with text labels and a tree fitted on shuffled labels as the floor. See Examples.

docs.title: Things to watch
docs.text:
• X_train for the slack. Without it, the slack is in the raw units of each feature. A feature measured in thousands then dominates the distance to the thresholds. Pass the training rows, or scale=.
  • A floor for trees. There is no "untrained tree". A tree of the same depth fitted on shuffled labels is a useful floor: same structure, no signal.
  • Depth 1. The first layer has a single split. The path alone puts every object at one of two points, and only the slack spreads them. Expect the joint and path readings to differ little there, and more from depth 2 on.
  • Ensembles. Random forests and boosting are not single trees. Use fa.Interpreter with an extractor built from model.apply(X) (see Choosing a module).

docs.text:
Everything below is importable from the top-level package (import fannar as fa), except where a module path is shown. The pages are generated from the docstrings in src/fannar.

docs.text: One entry point per kind of data, each a subclass of Interpreter that only sets defaults and handles the inputs. The modules load on first access (fa.tabular, fa.image, fa.text, fa.tree), so import fannar stays light.

docs.text:
TabularInterpreter(

Bases: Interpreter

Interpreter for a PyTorch model over tabular rows.

Parameters:

def as_table(X, y=None, feature_names: Sequence[str] | None = None, class_names: Sequence[str] | None = None,
             classes: Sequence | None = None, dtype=np.float32):
    """``(X, y, feature_names, class_names)`` from arrays or pandas objects.

    Explicit ``feature_names``/``class_names`` take precedence over what the DataFrame and the labels
    provide. ``X`` becomes a ``dtype`` array (``float32`` by default, the usual dtype of a model).

    if hasattr(X, "columns") and feature_names is None:
        feature_names = [str(c) for c in X.columns]
    if hasattr(X, "to_numpy"):
        X = X.to_numpy()
    if not hasattr(X, "detach"):  # leave tensors to the model's own dtype handling
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=dtype)
    y, names = encode_labels(y, classes)
    return X, y, feature_names, class_names if class_names is not None else names

def encode_labels(y, classes: Sequence | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray | None, list[str] | None]:
    """``y`` as class indices ``0 .. K-1`` plus the class names, when ``y`` is not already numeric.

    A pandas categorical keeps its category order. Strings, objects and booleans are matched against
    ``classes`` when given (e.g. ``tree.classes_``), otherwise against their sorted unique values, the
    same order as scikit-learn's ``LabelEncoder``. Numeric labels are returned unchanged with no names.
    """
    if y is None:
        return None, None
    cat = getattr(y, "cat", None)
    if cat is not None and str(getattr(y, "dtype", "")) == "category":
        return np.asarray(cat.codes, dtype=np.int64), [str(c) for c in cat.categories]
    y = np.asarray(y)
    if classes is not None:
        classes = np.asarray(classes)
        if np.issubdtype(classes.dtype, np.integer) and np.array_equal(classes, np.arange(len(classes))):
            return y, None
        index = {c: t for t, c in enumerate(classes.tolist())}
        unknown = sorted({str(c) for c in y.tolist() if c not in index})
        if unknown:
            raise ValueError(f"labels {unknown[:5]} are not among the model's classes {classes.tolist()}")
        return np.array([index[c] for c in y.tolist()], dtype=np.int64), [str(c) for c in classes]
    if np.issubdtype(y.dtype, np.number):
        return y, None
    names, codes = np.unique(y, return_inverse=True)
    return codes.astype(np.int64), [str(c) for c in names]

def block_names(model) -> list[str]:
    """Names of the children of the longest ``nn.ModuleList`` in ``model``: the transformer blocks.

    Raises ``ValueError`` when the model has no ``nn.ModuleList``; pass ``layers=`` explicitly then.
    """
    _need_torch()
    lists = [(name, m) for name, m in model.named_modules() if isinstance(m, nn.ModuleList) and len(m)]
    if not lists:
        raise ValueError("no nn.ModuleList found in the model; pass `layers=` explicitly")
    name, blocks = max(lists, key=lambda item: len(item[1]))  # first of the longest, in module order
    return [f"{name}.{t}" if name else str(t) for t in range(len(blocks))]

docs.title: Explanations
docs.text:
Why was this object classified differently from that one? (contrastive, per feature)

For a pair (i, j) and each feature f, x_i^(f) is x_i with feature f replaced by its value in x_j, and

Delta d_f = d(i, j) - d(i^(f), j)

in the representation space of each layer (positive: the swap brings i closer to j). Only the F + 2 rows x_j, x_i, x_i^(1..F) go through the model, so the cost is linear in the number of features. The ranking is validated outside the geometry by the swap test: copy the top-k features of j into i and check whether the model's prediction becomes the prediction of j (the procedure of nearest-instance counterfactuals such as NICE).

Delta d is first order: features that only matter jointly with others get no credit.

ErrorExplanation aggregates the same scores over the model's errors: each misclassified object is paired with the nearest object the model gets right in its true class, so the shares say which features keep the errors away from where they belong.

def direction(self, layer: str | None = None, mask=None) -> np.ndarray:
    """Share-weighted mean of ``sign(x_j - x_i)`` per feature, in ``[-1, 1]``: ``+1`` when the
    errors have lower values than their partners (raising the feature moves them towards
    their true class), ``-1`` when they have higher values."""
    s, d = self.shares[layer or self.layers[-1]], np.sign(self.xj - self.xi)
    if mask is not None:
        s, d = s[mask], d[mask]
    w = s.sum(0)
    return np.where(w > 0, (s * d).sum(0) / np.maximum(w, 1e-300), 0.0)

def pair_scores(extractor, pipeline, xi, xj, layers=None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """``Delta d_f`` per layer, from the ``F + 2`` swap rows."""
    xi, xj = np.asarray(xi, float).ravel(), np.asarray(xj, float).ravel()
    src = extractor(swap_rows(xi, xj).astype(np.float32))
    out = {}
    for layer in layers or src.layer_names:
        sources = src.layers[layer]
        if all(np.array_equal(a, np.broadcast_to(a[:1], a.shape)) for a in sources.values()):
            out[layer] = np.zeros(len(xi))  # every row has the same sources: nothing separates i from j here
            continue
        d = pipeline(sources=sources, keep_components=False).distances[0]
        out[layer] = d[1] - d[2:]
    return out

def swap_rows(xi: np.ndarray, xj: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """``[x_j, x_i, x_i^(1), ..., x_i^(F)]``."""
    F = len(xi)
    swapped = np.repeat(xi[None], F, axis=0)
    swapped[np.arange(F), np.arange(F)] = xj
    return np.concatenate([xj[None], xi[None], swapped])

def swap_curve(predict, xi, xj, target: int, order) -> np.ndarray:
    """For ``k = 0..F``: 1 if ``x_i`` with the first ``k`` features of ``order`` taken from
    ``x_j`` is predicted as ``target``. ``predict(X) -> labels``."""
    xi, xj = np.asarray(xi, float).ravel(), np.asarray(xj, float).ravel()
    F = len(xi)
    rank = np.empty(F, dtype=int)
    rank[np.asarray(order)] = np.arange(F)
    rows = np.repeat(xi[None], F + 1, axis=0)
    for k in range(F + 1):
        rows[k, rank < k] = xj[rank < k]
    return (np.asarray(predict(rows.astype(np.float32))) == target).astype(float)

def nearest_unlike(X, predictions, i: int) -> int:
    """The nearest object (Euclidean, in the given feature space) with another prediction."""
    X, predictions = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1), np.asarray(predictions)
    other = np.flatnonzero(predictions != predictions[i])
    if len(other) == 0:
        raise ValueError("every object has the same prediction")
    return int(other[np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(X[other] - X[i], axis=1))])

def nearest_correct(X, labels, predictions, i: int) -> int | None:
    """The nearest object (Euclidean, in the given feature space) correctly predicted as the
    true class of ``i``, or ``None`` if there is none."""
    X, labels, predictions = np.asarray(X, float).reshape(len(X), -1), np.asarray(labels), np.asarray(predictions)
    pool = np.flatnonzero((predictions == labels) & (labels == labels[i]))
    if len(pool) == 0:
        return None
    return int(pool[np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(X[pool] - X[i], axis=1))])

def __init__(self, model, X, y=None, *, layers: Sequence[str] | None = None,
             pipeline: KernelPipeline | str = "paper", reference_model=None,
             baselines: Sequence[KernelPipeline | str] | dict = ("activations",),
             extractor: Callable | None = None, feature_names: Sequence[str] | None = None,
             class_names: Sequence[str] | None = None, k: int = 5, **source_options) -> None:
    self.model, self.X, self.k = model, X, k
    self.y = None if y is None else np.asarray(y)
    self.feature_names = list(feature_names) if feature_names is not None else None
    self.class_names = list(class_names) if class_names is not None else None
    self.extractor = self._make_extractor(model, extractor, layers, source_options)
    self.reference_extractor = (None if reference_model is None
                                else self._make_extractor(reference_model, None, layers, source_options))
    self.pipeline = get_pipeline(pipeline)
    if _is_sklearn_tree(model) and pipeline == "paper":
        self.pipeline = KernelPipeline(["path", "slack", "classes"])
        if tuple(baselines) == ("activations",):
            baselines = {"path": KernelPipeline(["path"])}
    if isinstance(baselines, dict):
        self.baselines = {k: get_pipeline(v) for k, v in baselines.items()}
    else:
        self.baselines = {(b if isinstance(b, str) else f"baseline{t}"): get_pipeline(b)
                          for t, b in enumerate(baselines)}
    self.sources: Sources | None = None
    self.reference_sources: Sources | None = None
    self.spaces: dict[str, GramSpace] = {}

def evaluate(self, layers: Sequence[str] | None = None, include_baselines: bool = True,
             include_floor: bool = True) -> Report:
    """Behaviour readings per layer for the joint space, the baselines and the floor.

    The floor uses the reference model's *geometry* against the trained model's *behaviour*
    (the "cross" floor), so the only difference between a reading and its floor is training.
    """
    self._ensure()
    if self.y is None:
        raise ValueError("evaluate() needs the true labels `y`")
    layers = list(layers or self.layers)
    preds, probs = self.sources.predictions, self.sources.probabilities
    run = lambda sp: evaluate_space(sp, self.y, preds, probs, self.k)  # noqa: E731
    values = {"joint": {layer: run(self.spaces[layer]) for layer in layers}}
    if include_baselines:
        for name in self.baselines:
            ok = [layer for layer in layers if self._has(self.baselines[name], layer)]
            if ok:
                values[name] = {layer: run(self.baseline_space(name, layer)) for layer in ok}
    if include_floor and self.reference_sources is not None:
        values["floor"] = {layer: run(self.floor_space(layer)) for layer in layers}
    accuracy = float((preds == self.y).mean())
    return Report(layers, values, {"accuracy": accuracy, "n": len(self.y), "pipeline": repr(self.pipeline)})

def explain_errors(self, layers: Sequence[str] | None = None, against: str = "correct",
                   max_errors: int | None = None, reference: int = 100, seed: int = 0) -> ErrorExplanation:
    """Which features drive the model's errors, aggregated over the misclassified objects.

    Each error ``i`` is explained as a pair against a partner ``j``: with ``against="correct"``
    (default) the nearest object correctly predicted as the true class of ``i`` (falling back
    to the nearest unlike object when that class has none), so the shares say which features
    keep ``i`` away from its class in the representation space; with ``against="unlike"``, the
    nearest object with another prediction, as in :meth:`explain_pair`. ``max_errors`` caps the
    number of errors and ``reference`` the number of correctly predicted objects explained the
    same way as a baseline (both sampled with ``seed``; ``reference=0`` skips it).
    Vector inputs only."""
    if self.y is None:
        raise ValueError("explaining errors needs the true labels `y`")
    if against not in ("correct", "unlike"):
        raise ValueError("against must be 'correct' or 'unlike'")
    self._ensure()
    X, pred, rng = self._matrix(), self.predictions, np.random.default_rng(seed)
    errors = np.flatnonzero(pred != self.y)
    if len(errors) == 0:
        raise ValueError("the model makes no errors on these objects")
    if max_errors is not None and len(errors) > max_errors:
        errors = np.sort(rng.choice(errors, size=max_errors, replace=False))
    partners = []
    for i in errors:
        j = nearest_correct(X, self.y, pred, int(i)) if against == "correct" else None
        partners.append(nearest_unlike(X, pred, int(i)) if j is None else j)
    partners = np.array(partners)
    correct = np.flatnonzero(pred == self.y)
    correct = np.sort(rng.choice(correct, size=min(reference, len(correct)), replace=False))
    return ErrorExplanation(errors, partners, self.y[errors], pred[errors],
                            self._pair_shares(X, errors, partners, layers), X[errors], X[partners],
                            self._pair_shares(X, correct, [nearest_unlike(X, pred, int(i)) for i in correct], layers),
                            {int(c): int((self.y == c).sum()) for c in np.unique(self.y)},
                            self.feature_names, self.class_names)

def swap_test(self, pairs: int | Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = 50, layer: str | None = None,
              predict: Callable | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict:
    """Swap-test area per ranking (method, |Delta x|, random among differing features),
    averaged over pairs. ``pairs`` is a number of random correctly-predicted objects (each with
    its nearest unlike neighbour) or explicit ``(i, j)`` pairs."""
    self._ensure()
    X = self._matrix()
    predict = predict or self._predict_fn()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if isinstance(pairs, int):
        pool = np.flatnonzero(self.predictions == self.y) if self.y is not None else np.arange(len(X))
        chosen = rng.choice(pool, size=min(pairs, len(pool)), replace=False)
        pairs = [(int(i), nearest_unlike(X, self.predictions, int(i))) for i in chosen]
    layer = layer or self.layers[-1]
    areas = {"method": [], "absdiff": [], "random": []}
    for i, j in pairs:
        s = pair_scores(self.extractor, self.pipeline, X[i], X[j], [layer])[layer]
        differ = np.flatnonzero(np.abs(X[j] - X[i]) > 1e-12)
        rest = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(X.shape[1]), differ)
        orders = {"method": np.argsort(-s, kind="stable"), "absdiff": np.argsort(-np.abs(X[j] - X[i]), kind="stable"),
                  "random": np.concatenate([rng.permutation(differ), rest])}
        for key, order in orders.items():
            areas[key].append(curve_area(swap_curve(predict, X[i], X[j], int(self.predictions[j]), order)))
    return {k: float(np.mean(v)) for k, v in areas.items()} | {"pairs": len(pairs), "layer": layer}

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
Positive-definite kernels that turn one source of information into a raw Gram matrix.

Every kernel maps a set of objects X (any array-like whose first axis indexes the objects; the remaining axes are flattened) to the raw Gram matrix K[i, j] = kappa(x_i, x_j). The method only requires each kernel to be positive definite; which kernel to use is part of the instantiation, not of the method.

A word on composition. The joint Gram is the Hadamard product of the component Grams. With linear-type kernels this realises the tensor product of the feature spaces, so the joint similarity keeps the multiplicative interaction between sources. With Gaussian kernels it does not: the product of two Gaussians is the Gaussian of the summed exponents, and the composition collapses into an additive combination of the source metrics. RBF is available, but Linear/Cosine are the default for this reason.

def compute(self, X, Y):
    nx = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)
    ny = np.linalg.norm(Y, axis=1)
    k = (X @ Y.T) / np.maximum(np.outer(nx, ny), self.eps)
    if X is Y:

    return k

def compute(self, X, Y):
    sx = (X**2).sum(1)[:, None]
    sy = (Y**2).sum(1)[None, :]
    d2 = np.maximum(sx + sy - 2 * X @ Y.T, 0.0)
    gamma = self.gamma
    if gamma is None:
        med = np.median(d2[d2 > 0]) if np.any(d2 > 0) else 1.0
        gamma = 1.0 / med
    return np.exp(-gamma * d2)

The kernel-transformation pipeline: component Grams, Hadamard composition, final transform.

::

G = T( T_1(K_1) o T_2(K_2) o ... o T_d(K_d) )

def component_grams(self, sources: Mapping | None = None, grams: Mapping | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """``T_l(K_l)`` for every component. A raw Gram in ``grams`` takes precedence over the
    kernel applied to ``sources``, so any component can be replaced by the user's own matrix."""
    sources, grams = sources or {}, grams or {}
    out = {}
    for name, comp in self.components.items():
        if name in grams:
            raw = np.asarray(grams[name], dtype=np.float64)
        elif name in sources:
            raw = comp.kernel(sources[name])
        else:
            raise KeyError(f"no source or Gram given for component {name!r}")
        out[name] = comp.transform(raw)
    return out

def plot_report(report: Report, readings=None):
    """One panel per reading, one line per representation, layers on the x axis. Readings that are
    undefined everywhere (e.g. the confusion agreement with fewer than 5 classes) are left out."""
    plt = _plt()

def plot_embedding(rows: dict, layers: list, colors, labels=None, predictions=None, class_names=None):
    """The space of each layer projected on its two dominant modes (kernel PCA of G).

    ``rows`` maps a row name to one :class:`GramSpace` per layer. Colour = ``colors`` (predicted
    class by default); ``x`` marks the model's errors when labels are known."""
    plt = _plt()
    colors = np.asarray(colors)
    classes = np.unique(colors)
    palette = dict(zip(classes, _class_colors(len(classes))))
    wrong = None if labels is None or predictions is None else np.asarray(predictions) != np.asarray(labels)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), len(layers), figsize=(1.9 * len(layers), 1.9 * len(rows) + 0.5), squeeze=False)
    for r, (name, spaces) in enumerate(rows.items()):
        for c, sp in enumerate(spaces):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            xy, frac = sp.embedding(2)
            ok = np.ones(len(xy), bool) if wrong is None else ~wrong
            for cls in classes:
                m = (colors == cls) & ok
                ax.scatter(xy[m, 0], xy[m, 1], s=4, color=palette[cls], linewidths=0, alpha=0.85)
            if wrong is not None:
                ax.scatter(xy[wrong, 0], xy[wrong, 1], s=10, marker="x", color="black", linewidths=0.6)
            ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
            ax.text(0.02, 0.02, f"{frac:.0%}", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=6, color="0.35")
            if r == 0:
                ax.set_title(str(layers[c]), fontsize=8)
            if c == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(name, fontsize=8)
    handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], ls="none", marker="o", ms=4, color=palette[c],
                          label=(class_names[c] if class_names is not None and np.issubdtype(type(c), np.integer) else str(c)))
               for c in classes[:20]]
    if wrong is not None:

    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=min(len(handles), 11), fontsize=7, frameon=False,

    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1))

def plot_gram(space, order_by=None):

def plot_errors(expl, k: int | None = None, layer: str | None = None, rows: str = "class"):
    """Which features the model's errors hinge on, by true class (``rows="class"``) or by
    true→predicted confusion (``rows="confusion"``).

    * matrix: columns are the features (the ``k`` with the largest mean share over all errors),
      cells the mean share of the feature among the row's errors, with an arrow for the direction
      (↑: the errors have lower values than the nearest correct object of their true class; ↓:
      higher);
    * top: mean share over the errors against the mean share over correctly predicted objects
      (how much the feature matters to the model in general);
    * right: errors per row, and the error rate of the class (or the fraction of all errors).
    """
    plt = _plt()
    layer = layer or expl.layers[-1]
    cols = expl.ranking(layer)[:k]
    names = [expl.names[f] for f in cols]
    cname = (lambda c: str(expl.class_names[c])) if expl.class_names else (lambda c: f"class {c}")
    if rows == "class":
        keys = sorted(expl.support) or sorted(set(expl.true.tolist()))
        masks = [expl.true == c for c in keys]
        labels = [cname(c) for c in keys]
        totals = [expl.support.get(c, int(m.sum())) for c, m in zip(keys, masks)]
    elif rows == "confusion":
        confs = expl.confusions()
        masks = [(expl.true == a) & (expl.pred == b) for a, b, _ in confs]
        labels = [f"{cname(a)} → {cname(b)}" for a, b, _ in confs]
        totals = [len(expl.errors)] * len(confs)
    else:
        raise ValueError("rows must be 'class' or 'confusion'")
    mat = np.full((len(masks), len(cols)), np.nan)
    arrows = np.zeros_like(mat)
    for r, m in enumerate(masks):
        if m.any():
            mat[r], arrows[r] = expl.mean_shares(layer, m)[cols], expl.direction(layer, m)[cols]

    nr, nc = len(masks), len(cols)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(max(7.5, 0.8 * nc + 4.2), 2.6 + 0.48 * nr))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1.7, max(0.48 * nr, 1.2)], width_ratios=[0.8 * nc, 2.6],
                          hspace=0.08, wspace=0.05)
    ax_top, ax_note = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    ax_mat = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0], sharex=ax_top)
    ax_rate = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1], sharey=ax_mat)

    x = np.arange(nc)
    err_share, ref = expl.mean_shares(layer)[cols], expl.reference_shares(layer)
    width = 0.38 if ref is not None else 0.6
    ax_top.bar(x - (width / 2 if ref is not None else 0), err_share, width, color=OKABE_ITO[0], label="over the errors")
    if ref is not None:
        ax_top.bar(x + width / 2, ref[cols], width, color="0.75", label="over correct predictions")
    for t, v in enumerate(err_share):
        ax_top.text(t - (width / 2 if ref is not None else 0), v, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7)
    top = max(err_share.max(), 0 if ref is None else ref[cols].max())
    ax_top.set_ylim(0, top * 1.25 + 1e-12)
    ax_top.set_ylabel("mean share", fontsize=8)
    ax_top.set_title(f"features behind the errors · layer {layer} · {len(expl.errors)} errors", fontsize=9, loc="left")
    ax_top.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
    ax_top.tick_params(labelbottom=False)
    _style(ax_top)

    cmap = _plt().get_cmap("Blues").with_extremes(bad="0.94")
    vmax = max(np.nanmax(mat) if np.isfinite(mat).any() else 0, 1e-12)
    ax_mat.imshow(np.ma.masked_invalid(mat), cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto")

            if np.isnan(v):
                continue
            a = arrows[r, c]
            mark = (" ↑" if a > 0 else " ↓") if abs(a) >= 1 / 3 and v >= 0.02 else ""
            ax_mat.text(c, r, f"{v:.0%}{mark}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                        color="white" if v > 0.6 * vmax else "0.15")

def auc(score, positive) -> float:
    """Area under the ROC curve of ``score`` for the boolean ``positive`` (Mann-Whitney)."""
    score, positive = np.asarray(score, float), np.asarray(positive, bool)
    pos, neg = score[positive], score[~positive]
    if len(pos) == 0 or len(neg) == 0:
        return float("nan")
    ranks = _rankdata(np.concatenate([pos, neg]))
    return float((ranks[: len(pos)].sum() - len(pos) * (len(pos) + 1) / 2) / (len(pos) * len(neg)))

def spearman(a, b) -> float:
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    ok = np.isfinite(a) & np.isfinite(b)
    a, b = a[ok], b[ok]
    if len(a) < 3 or np.std(a) == 0 or np.std(b) == 0:
        return float("nan")
    return float(np.corrcoef(_rankdata(a), _rankdata(b))[0, 1])

def knn_prediction(space, predictions, k: int = 5) -> float:
    """Leave-one-out k-NN accuracy of the space against the model's own predictions. O(n^2)."""
    d = _distances(space).copy()
    target = np.asarray(predictions)
    np.fill_diagonal(d, np.inf)
    k = min(k, len(d) - 1)
    nn = np.argpartition(d, k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]
    votes = target[nn]
    hits = 0
    for i in range(len(d)):
        vals, counts = np.unique(votes[i], return_counts=True)
        hits += int(vals[np.argmax(counts)] == target[i])
    return hits / len(d)

def class_distance_matrix(space, labels) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """``(K, K)`` mean distance between the objects of each pair of classes, and the classes."""
    d, labels = _distances(space), np.asarray(labels)
    classes = np.unique(labels)
    out = np.full((len(classes), len(classes)), np.nan)
    for a, ca in enumerate(classes):
        ia = labels == ca
        for b, cb in enumerate(classes):
            block = d[np.ix_(ia, labels == cb)]
            if a == b:
                m = ~np.eye(len(block), dtype=bool)
                out[a, b] = block[m].mean() if m.any() else 0.0
            else:
                out[a, b] = block.mean()
    return out, classes

def geometric_margin(space, labels, against=None) -> np.ndarray:
    """Per object, ``(d_near - d_own) / (d_near + d_own)`` in ``[-1, 1]``: mean distance to the
    closest competing class minus mean distance to the reference class (``against``, default the
    object's own label), over their sum. Positive inside the reference class's region."""
    d, labels = _distances(space), np.asarray(labels)
    classes = np.unique(labels)
    idx = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(classes)}
    d = d.copy()
    np.fill_diagonal(d, np.nan)  # an object's distance to itself is not evidence of anything
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):
        means = np.stack([np.nanmean(d[:, labels == c], axis=1) for c in classes], axis=1)
    means = np.nan_to_num(means, nan=0.0)
    own_cls = np.array([idx[c] for c in (labels if against is None else np.asarray(against))])
    rows = np.arange(len(d))
    own = means[rows, own_cls]
    other = means.copy()
    other[rows, own_cls] = np.inf
    near = other.min(1)
    return (near - own) / np.maximum(near + own, 1e-12)

def correctness_auc(space, labels, predictions) -> float:
    """How well the geometric margin predicts that the model is right.

    The margin groups objects by the model's *predictions*: the true labels only define the
    target (right or wrong). Using them in the margin as well would make the reading circular and
    would rely on a signal that does not exist at deployment time."""
    labels, predictions = np.asarray(labels), np.asarray(predictions)
    return auc(geometric_margin(space, predictions), predictions == labels)
